rules.statement: When the same contract (file names, encodings, environment variable names) is implemented in two places, such as a C# class and a build script, add a test that ties them together, for example a shared golden fixture that both sides' tests check against.
rules.why: Otherwise the two sides can drift apart while every test still passes, and the failure only shows up in a full end-to-end run with no hint of the cause.
rules.check: Look for a script or second-language copy of logic that a C# type also implements, with no test that compares its output to the C# side or to a shared fixture.

rules.statement: Don't hand-maintain a list in code that copies entries from a configuration file. Derive it from the config, or add a test that reads the config and asserts that the list matches it.
rules.why: If only comments keep the copies in step, an entry added to or renamed in the config gets skipped silently and causes failures that are hard to trace.
rules.check: Look for hard-coded id lists or names that mirror entries in an appsettings or other config file, with no derivation and no test comparing them.

rules.statement: Template expansion that substitutes placeholder tokens must fail and name the leftover tokens if any placeholder remains unreplaced after expansion.
rules.why: A misspelled or new token otherwise passes through as literal text and causes an unclear failure further down the line.
rules.check: Look for template code that calls Replace once per token and never checks the result for remaining `{{...}}` patterns.

rules.statement: Don't copy a helper function between build scripts. Move it into a shared script that each one dot-sources.
rules.why: If one copy changes, for example in its padding handling, the scripts can quietly produce different results.
rules.check: Look for the same function defined in more than one script file.

rules.statement: In a test project, each test asserts one behavior, the one its name describes. Move any extra assertion, such as a length check, into its own test named for that behavior.
rules.why: If the first assertion fails, the second never runs, and the test name describes only one of the two.
rules.check: Look for a test method that asserts two independent behaviors when its name mentions only one.

rules.statement: In a test project, use the constants and helper methods that the class under test exposes instead of repeating their string values as literals, except in a test that deliberately pins the exact shared contract.
rules.why: Tests that repeat literals go stale without a compiler error when a constant is renamed. A contract-pinning test has to spell the values out, though, because reading them from the class under test would make it tautological.
rules.check: Look for test literals that duplicate a public constant of the type under test. Before reporting, check whether the test exists to pin the exact external contract, which is often noted in a comment. Don't report it if it does.

rules.statement: Don't ask for a test of a thin wiring method, such as a loop of builder `WithEnvironment` calls, when it is marked `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` with a justification and the logic it applies is tested elsewhere.
rules.why: The maintainer declined this finding: the wiring itself carries little risk, and the tests on the method that builds its input already cover the behavior.
rules.check: Before reporting a missing test, check whether the method has `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage(Justification = ...)]` and only passes along data from a tested method.

rules.statement: Don't ask a consumer's tests to repeat coverage of a helper's edge case, such as replacing an empty file, when the helper's own tests already cover it.
rules.why: The maintainer answered that the case is covered where it lives, so the consumer tests don't need to repeat it.
rules.check: Before reporting an uncovered edge case of a helper that a consumer calls, look for that case in the helper's own tests in the same or a related test project.
